title: What the sea gave
hookLine: the treasures rise, and people read them two ways
carry: one story, read as holy event and inner path
tomorrow: the nectar's finally out, and everyone grabs. who gets a taste?

lines: DID IT HAPPEN, OR IS IT YOU?
cards: Kamadhenu, a cow that grants wishes. A white horse. Airavata, a white elephant.
A tree in flower. The moon. A great jewel.
Then, standing on a lotus, Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, who chooses Vishnu. Last of all comes Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, carrying the pot of amrita.
It reads like the end of a long quest when the loot finally drops. And people who love this story have a real argument about it: did this happen, or is it a picture of something inside you?

teach.b: The Puranas list the treasures a little differently, but the shape is the same: the sea gives, once the poison is behind it.

And the treasures are still on the calendar: Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, honors Dhanvantari rising with the amrita, and on Diwali night families worship Lakshmi. Now the two readings, each at its best.
The first: these are holy events. Vishnu really came down as the tortoise; Lakshmi really rose from the sea; the amrita is real. For devotees who hold this, the story isn't a code to crack.
It's the history of the gods, and part of why Lakshmi is worshipped and Vishnu trusted to hold the world. Turning it into a metaphor, this side says, shrinks the gods to fit inside your head.

The second: the churning is a picture of the inner life. Some teachers read the ocean as the mind, the churning as long practice, the poison as the hard stuff that surfaces first, and the nectar as freedom at the end.
On this reading the story belongs to anyone who has worked through something hard. Keeping it only as events, this side says, leaves it on a shelf.
Hindu tradition doesn't make you choose: one story can be holy history and an inner path at once, and many pray to Lakshmi and also hear the churning as their own story.
Both readings agree on the order: poison first, treasures after.

how: Dhanteras, two days before Diwali, honors Dhanvantari rising from the churned sea with the amrita, and Lakshmi is worshipped on Diwali night; some teachers also explain the churning as a picture of inner practice, and many families hold both readings without choosing.

o: the wish-granting cow that rises from the sea
the tortoise below while the sea gives up treasures
the jewel Vishnu wears after the great churning

p: rises on a lotus, chooses Vishnu

s: every Purana lists the treasures in exactly the same way
the lists differ a little; the shape, poison first and treasures after, stays.
Lakshmi rises from the churning sea and chooses Vishnu
she stands on a lotus and chooses him.
in the story, Kurma takes a treasure as his reward
nothing in the story says he takes one; he stays underneath.

games.q: your cousin says 'the churning is just a metaphor.' give the devotee's best case in one line.
o: it really happened; that's part of why Lakshmi is worshipped and Vishnu trusted.
metaphors are for people who don't really believe.
it's too old to know, so it doesn't matter either way.
games.why: that's the first reading at its best: holy events, not a code to crack. the other side's best case: the story belongs to anyone working through something hard.

practice: Pick up or look at one object near you: a ring, a mug, a photo. For the first half of the sit, see it only as a thing, its weight, its color, its edges.
For the second half, let it be what it stands for: who gave it, what it holds for you. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for both.

wordCard.voice: Kurma: the tortoise underneath the churning, while the treasures rise into the light.
